content: 1. Evidence suggests a significant linear association between sedentary behavior and measures of adiposity in adults. This relationship has been systematically reviewed and analyzed in various studies. 2. Ahmad et al. (2017) conducted a systematic review including 15 studies (1 prospective cohort, 1 case-control, and 13 cross-sectional studies) with a total of 13,395 participants. The majority of studies (13 out of 15) reported a significant positive association between higher sedentary time (ST) and body mass index (BMI), while 2 studies found no significant association. However, the evidence was rated as very low due to serious risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision. 3. Del Pozo-Cruz et al. (2018) reviewed six cross-sectional studies (N=4,774) that used accelerometers to measure sedentary time. The studies varied in their definitions of sedentary time, using thresholds of <100 counts per minute (cpm) for vertical axis data or <200 cpm for vector magnitude data. After removing one study contributing to statistical heterogeneity, the association between replacing sedentary time with moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and BMI was no longer statistically significant. The evidence was rated as very low due to serious bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. 4. Bailey et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to examine the relationship between total daily sitting time and the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetes. Nine prospective studies with 448,285 participants were included. Higher levels of sitting time were associated with an increased risk of CVD and diabetes, independent of physical activity levels. The findings suggest that reducing total daily sitting time may be beneficial for public health. 5. Berger et al. (2019) analyzed data from 12 prospective cohort studies (30,810 prostate cancer cases) to investigate the relationship between sedentary behavior and prostate cancer. Sedentary behavior was not independently associated with prostate cancer overall. However, prolonged sedentary behavior may increase the risk of aggressive prostate cancer through mechanisms involving obesity. This highlights the potential importance of sedentary behavior as a modifiable risk factor for aggressive prostate cancer. 6. Chan et al. (2019) systematically reviewed 126 observational cohort studies on physical activity, sedentary behavior, adiposity, and breast cancer risk. Higher physical activity was inversely associated with both preand postmenopausal breast cancer, while increased sitting time was positively associated with postmenopausal breast cancer. Adult weight gain and greater body adiposity increased breast cancer risk in postmenopausal women, particularly for hormone receptor-positive (HR+) cancers. The evidence was less consistent for premenopausal women. 7. Del Pozo-Cruz et al. (2018) conducted a meta-analysis of studies using device-based measurements to examine the effects of replacing sedentary time with physical activity. Reallocating 30 minutes of sedentary time to light-intensity physical activity was associated with reductions in waist circumference, fasting insulin, and all-cause mortality risk, as well as an increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Replacing sedentary time with MVPA showed stronger and broader benefits, including reductions in BMI, fasting glucose, and all-cause mortality. These findings suggest that even light-intensity activity can be beneficial, particularly for individuals unable to engage in higher-intensity activities. 8. Ekelund et al. (2019) performed a systematic review and harmonized meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies to examine dose-response associations between accelerometer-measured physical activity, sedentary time, and all-cause mortality. Higher levels of physical activity, regardless of intensity, were associated with lower mortality risk, while greater sedentary time was linked to higher mortality risk. These findings emphasize the importance of reducing sedentary time and increasing physical activity to improve overall health outcomes.
